newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Taleban send reinforcements to Afghan fronts.
newsitem.headline: Taleban send reinforcements to Afghan fronts.

text.p: Afghan opposition commander Ahmad Shah Masood still controlled access to the vital Salang Pass on Thursday, despite attempts by the Taleban militia to open up the main road between Kabul and the north.
A military source said the purist Islamic militia had failed to dislodge Masood's guerrillas from the strategic town of Jabal-os-Siraj at the foot of the Salang Pass.
"Masood still controls the tactical parts of the town and has control of the road," the source said. "The Salang highway is not only firmly defended, it's also blocked."
The source, who asked not to be named, said Masood's men also held most of the nearby village of Golbahar, at the entrance to the guerrilla chief's Panjsher Valley stronghold.
Taleban officials said on Wednesday that their forces controlled all of Golbahar and most of Jabal-os-Siraj.
The Pakistan-based Afghan Islamic Press (AIP) news service said more fighting was under way around Jabal-os-Siraj, 70 km (44 miles) north of Kabul, on Thursday, but had no details.
It said opposition fighters were tightening pressure on a Taleban force that crossed the Salang Pass over the Hindu Kush mountains last week, but is now effectively cut off.
The Taleban had been able to get through the Salang because of the apparent defection of one of Masood's top lieutenants, Basir Salangi, since reported to have gone back to Masood.

AIP said Salangi was now claiming that his defection to the Taleban was a ruse intended to lead to the capture of several Taleban leaders. The trick failed to net senior Taleban figures, but Salangi said he had captured 150 of the militia's fighters.

AIP said troops loyal to ethnic Uzbek General Abdul Malik were attacking the Taleban on Thursday in the hilly Robatak area, 30 km (19 miles) northwest of Pul-i-Khumri, where the stranded Taleban force of 2,000 to 3,000 men is based.

The Taleban moved over the Salang Pass to try to link up with their comrades who briefly took over the northern capital of Mazar-i-Sharif after allying with Malik to drive opposition leader General Abdul Rashid Dostum into exile.

But Malik turned against the Taleban and joined forces with an opposition Shi'ite Moslem militia to push them out of Mazar-i-Sharif after bloody street battles in which the Taleban lost at least 300 dead and 700 captured.
The prisoners include Taleban Foreign Minister Mullah Mohamamd Ghous, northern commander Mullah Abdul Razzaq and central bank chief Mullah Ahsanullah.
Following their military setbacks in the north, the Taleban launched a recruiting drive in Islamic religious schools in Pakistan and southern Afghanistan.
AIP said a truck convoy of about 1,300 Taleban left the eastern town of Khost for Kabul on Wednesday to join the battle against what their commander called "communist elements".
Maulvi Jallaluddin Haqqani, a veteran guerrilla commander from the struggle against Soviet troops in the 1980s, told the reinforcements that they were fighting a new jihad (holy war).
"There is again an imminent danger of division of our country because of communist elements who are occupying northern parts of Afghanistan and a jihad is a must now," he said.

Haqqani, some of whose men are already fighting in the Jabal-os-Siraj area, said Masood, renowned for his guerrilla exploits against the former Red Army, was now supporting communists and had closed the Salang highway. "Therefore a jihad must be waged against Masood," Haqqani declared, adding that he would go in person to the frontline.
The Taleban, who seized Kabul in September, are trying to impose strict Islamic rule throughout war-ravaged Afghanistan.
